newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo first half agriculture exports below target.
newsitem.headline: Yugo first half agriculture exports below target.

text.p: The performance of the agriculture and food sector over the first six months of this year has dampened hopes that it will take the lead in Yugoslav export growth, analysts said on Monday.
"Agriculture's performance in the first half of 1997 is much worse than in the second half of 1996," Vojislav Stankovic of the Institute for Foreign Trade told Reuters.

The agriculture and food industry exported goods worth $213.4 million in January-June, or 20.8 percent of total Yugoslav commodity exports. Imports were worth $328.2 million or 15.5 percent of commodity imports.
Agricultural exports include wheat, medicinal herbs fruit and vegetables, tobacco and cigarettes, livestock, processed meats, wine and sugar.

A slowdown in exports and considerable growth in imports have resulted in a trade gap of $114.8 million in the first half of this year in the agriculture and food sector, the Institute said in its latest report.
"The rates of import growth and export slowdown are both around 24 percent compared to the second half of 1996," Stankovic said.
Yugoslavia's total first half trade gap stood at $1.084 billion, with exports worth $1.028 billion and imports $2.112 billion.
The government has set a target of $700 million for agriculture and food exports for 1997.
The Yugoslav government recently introduced a surtax on imports of some agricultural and food products to protect domestic producers.
But analysts said these were not enough to protect the domestic market from imports from countries where agriculture and food industries are heavily subsidised.
Yugoslavia subidises its agricultural exports to the tune of one to three percent of their price at the time they leave the country, but subsidises are irregularly paid.

"How do you explain a surtax of 0.10 dinars per kilo of wheat if the present world price is 0.70-0.90 dinars per kilo compared to 1.40 dinars per kilo it is currently quoted at on the Novi Sad commodity exchange," Stankovic said.
As other examples, the institute cited lack of surtax on fruit and vegetables and low surtax on meat and meat products.
"We are not sure certain levels of surtax are protecting our producers, for example there is no surtax on unrefined sugar," Stankovic said.
Excessive imports of raw sugar are seen as the reason for a reduction in Yugoslav 1997 sugar beet area to some 58,000 ha from the planned 100,000 ha.

"The federal government's decision on surtax appears aimed more at filling up certain budget deficits than at protecting domestic producers," Stankovic said. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 311 4305
